June 9, 2026 
 
Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA 
 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
 
RE: CMS-0062-P 
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
Thank you for your leadership on coverage, access and patient care issues. On behalf of 
the Pulmonary Hypertension Association (PHA) and the pulmonary hypertension (PH) 
community, I write today to provide comment on the recent proposed rule, CMS-0062-P: 
2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs. 
 
PHA applauds your commitment to improving electronic prior authorization so patients 
and providers can benefit from a more expeditious, transparent and reliable process. In 
these comments, we outline how streamlined, electronic prior authorization, when 
implemented correctly, can improve and even extend the lives of individuals with 
pulmonary hypertension.  
 
Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) and the Pulmonary Hypertension Association (PHA) 
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) describes high blood pressure in the lungs, which can 
occur without a known cause, or in conjunction with underlying heart, lung or 
rheumatologic disease, blood clots in the lungs, or sleep disordered breathing. The disease 
can impact anyone of any age. Without prompt, appropriate treatment, PH can be rapidly 
progressive and fatal.  
 
The World Health Organization divides PH into five types, or groups. In many cases, PH  
is a complex, progressive and frequently fatal condition with available treatments but no 
cure. Delayed access to the most appropriate, highest impact treatment, whether from 
misdiagnosis or benefits management requirements, can lead to loss of function that is not 
always recovered even after appropriate therapy is started. In the worst-case scenario, 
delayed access to appropriate therapy can lead to death.  
 
PH requires careful management by a specialist care team. Available therapy options 
address four distinct disease pathways and are frequently used in combination for 
maximum clinical effectiveness. Delivery mechanism varies by therapy and is sometimes 
quite complex. Treatment for advanced PAH often includes an around-the-clock infusion 
directly into the patientâ€™s heart administered via a pump the patient carries with them at 
all times. Oral, inhaled, injected and short-term infusion treatment options are also 
prescribed.  
 
 
Due to the complex nature of the disease, appropriate therapy varies by patient, even among 
individuals with similar clinical presentation. In addition, some PH patients have dramatic 
responses to even small changes in treatment, such as the small differences between brand and 
generic therapy. When ideal therapy is delayed or disrupted, patients may experience a rapid 
health decline leading to emergency room visits, loss in functional ability and possibly a 
permanent transition to more aggressive, costly treatment.  
 
The Pulmonary Hypertension Association (PHA) is the country's leading PH 
organization. PHA's mission is to extend and improve the lives of those affected by PH. 
PHA is a unique, multi-stakeholder organization serving health care professionals as well 
as patients and their loved ones. PHA accredits PH clinical programs, coordinates a 
national observational patient registry and offers a robust continuing medical education 
program. In addition, the organization provides peer support groups, online and in-person 
education and advocacy opportunities to people living with PH and their loved ones.   
 
Impact of Prior Authorization on Patient Care 
In a 2023 survey of PHA Accredited Care Centersâ€™ experiences with prior authorization, PHA 
received responses from 79 health care providers representing 66 medical practices in 33 states. 
72% of respondents saw 90% or more of their authorization requests eventually approved, but to 
reach that endpoint, nearly half (48%) of centers dedicated 20 hours/week or more of staff time 
to managing prior authorization and re-authorization of PH therapy. A dozen centers reported 
staff spending 41-60 hours/week, on these tasks, diminishing the time available to engage 
directly with patients.  
 
Health care professionals described multiple barriers to successful treatment authorization for 
PH, a rapidly progressive, life-threatening condition:  
ï‚· Technology is often antiquated, failing to align with electronic medical record systems. 
ï‚· Authorization requirements and paperwork vary by payer even for the same drugs. 
ï‚· Authorization requirements often lag behind current clinical guidelines, sometimes by 
many years. 
ï‚· Authorization forms for PH therapy often request test results or other information that are 
not relevant to diagnosing the disease, making it challenging, or even impossible to 
complete the form. 
 
When these challenges result in the need for an appeal, new barriers arise: 
ï‚· Initial denials may not include clear guidance about the reason for the denial. 
ï‚· The health care professional reviewing the case may lack expertise in pulmonary 
hypertension. 
ï‚· Payers who provided an initial denial in a matter of days may take weeks, or even 
months, to respond to appeals.  
ï‚· Peer-to-peer discussions between the treating physician and the appeal reviewer are 
difficult to schedule and cause further treatment delays. 
 
Providers communicated that even after an authorization was approved, it had to be renewed 
every six to twelve months, sometimes disrupting therapy that the patient in question had been 
doing well on for years.  
 
A majority of health care professional survey respondents (63%) indicated that 
authorization requirements â€œoftenâ€ or â€œalwaysâ€ delayed their patientsâ€™ access to needed 
care. The most common impacts of this delayed care were unnecessary extensions of hospital 
stays (80%), worsening of PH symptoms caused by running out of or delaying the start of a drug 
(84%), and the mental distress patients and their families and caregivers experience (91%). 
Taken together, these impacts of delayed care lead to increased long-term costs to the health care 
system. 
 
Expedited Review & Limited Redetermination  
Since PH is a rapidly progressive and fatal condition, we are supportive of the American Medical 
Associationâ€™s (AMA) 48-hour recommendation for standard reviews. PHA also supports a 24-
hour recommendation for expedited reviews, particularly for progressive conditions like PH.  
 
PHA believes that 24â€“48-hour time limits should apply to almost all interactions between payers 
and health care professionals for urgent prior authorization cases, including appeals. In cases 
where engagement from a disease expert is needed to review an appeal, the process should be 
handled as promptly as possible, and within no more than 72 hours. 
 
PH health care professionals have reported disingenuous tactics from payers, such as demanding 
information for reviews over the weekend when there is no one available to respond within the 
timeline and using this as a reason to deny a request. These tactics are harmful to patient 
outcomes and should be prohibited. 
 
In addition, PHA supports longer periods of time between prior authorization renewals. For PH 
patients who have switched insurance plans, there should be at least three months before 
authorization is required, with the ideal timeframe being at least six months.  
 
For standard re-authorization, PH health care professionals have indicated that re-authorization 
every six to twelve months is disruptive for patients who are stable and effectively treated on 
their current therapies. Given the life-long, incurable nature of PH, renewals every three to five 
years are more appropriate. Longer times between re-authorization reduce unnecessary burden 
on health care professionals and patients.   
 
APIs, Electronic Medical Records and Artificial Intelligence  
PHA supports health care professionals having the ability to track all prior authorizations 
electronically and applauds the administration for this approach to streamlining the prior 
authorization process. To be effective, electronic health records technology must be fully capable 
of documenting complex medical testing such as echocardiograms and right heart 
catheterizations as these are critical tests for PH patients.  
 
Form standardization can also play an important role in streamlining the prior authorization 
process. However, a standardized form must be structured in a way that does not require health 
information that is irrelevant to the specific diagnosis for which the therapy is being prescribed.  
 
PHA supports full transparency during the prior authorization process regarding who is 
conducting reviews of both initial requests and appeals and clear reasons for any denials. In cases 
where artificial intelligence makes an initial denial, a review of the decision by an expert, human 
health care professional should happen automatically, without requiring an appeal.  
 
Additional Recommendations  
PHA recommends a gold carding approach to reducing prior authorization barriers and 
maximizing effective care for individuals with PH treated at an accredited center of care. Careful 
consideration should be given to the required approval rate, as many authorization requests are 
initially denied based on minor administrative errors rather than actual misalignment with 
treatment guidelines. A 90% required approval rate to be eligible for gold status should focus on 
eventual approval, not approval on first submission. 
 
PHA believes in the importance of access to real-time formulary information for health care 
professionals and patients. For PH patients, comprehensive formulary information should be 
available before the selection of a plan as many patients will inadvertently choose plans that do 
not fulfil their medical needs due to a lack of accessible information before enrollment.  
 
Streamlining Step Therapy Through Technology  
PHA applauds CMS for seeking additional comment about step therapy. PH is a progressive, 
often fatal condition, with common initial symptoms such as shortness of breath and fatigue. As 
a result, PH is commonly misdiagnosed and most patients are in an advanced state of the 
condition by the time they receive a correct diagnosis.  
 
In this context, step therapy requirements can further delay appropriate treatment, leading to 
irreversible decline and increased costs to the health care system. PHA urges preserving the 
integrity of expert clinical judgement and the physician-patient relationship by excluding payers 
from treatment decision making. Technology should only be used to advance access to necessary 
medications for patients, as any delays in care can result in increased costs to the health care 
system and devastating health outcomes.  
 
Specifically, PHA encourages CMS to: 
ï‚· Require plans to implement a step therapy exceptions process. Require all health 
insurance plans under its jurisdiction to offer a clear, medically reasonable, and expedient 
exceptions process to step therapy. This exceptions process should require plans to 
respond to urgent requests within 24 hours and within 72 hours for normal requests. 
Exceptions to step therapy should be allowed in the following five circumstances: 
o The patient already tried the insurance-preferred drug, and it has failed or is 
reasonably expected to be ineffective. 
o Delayed treatment will cause irreversible health consequences. 
o The insurance planâ€™s preferred drug is contraindicated or will likely cause harm to 
the patient. 
o Required drug will decrease the patientâ€™s ability to work, attend school, or fulfill 
activities of daily living. 
o The patient is stable on their current medication. 
ï‚· Require recognition of previous payerâ€™s step therapy determination: We recommend 
CMS require that new payers apply the previous payerâ€™s determination that a patient has 
satisfied step therapy and grant immediate access to any prescribed medication. 
Treatment disruptions that occur when patients are forced to repeat step therapy can be 
devastating for PH patients.  
 
ï‚· Standardize a step therapy exceptions process across payers: Similar to the prior 
authorization process, step therapy should have a uniform exceptions process across all 
payers to increase efficiency. A step therapy exceptions process should:  
o Allow the provider to present their clinical rationale for the request. 
o Require more transparency for the process such as the clinical reasoning for the 
step therapy protocols and any rationale for declining a request. 
o Requiring a detailed explanation of the appeals process after any denials. 
o Require that any denial made by AI receive an automatic review from an expert, 
human physician without requiring an appeal.  
o Standardize prior authorization and re-authorization requirements for each drug so 
that they are the same across all payers and in line with current clinical guidelines. 
o Create a standardized authorization form that is used by all payers, with attention 
given to making sure the uniform requirements require only information and test 
results appropriate for a given diagnosis.  
o Standardize the step therapy exceptions process including expedited review 
timelines for step therapy exceptions request. 
 
Technology should be used in this effort to streamline step therapy exceptions and CMS should 
create a platform that ensures step therapy information and the exceptions process are 
standardized across payers. Technology is essential to streamlining the process in a manner that 
makes our healthcare system more efficient, transparent and patient-centric. 
 
Thank you for your time and for your consideration of PHAâ€™s input. We remain hopeful that our 
views and recommendations will be reflected in any final rule.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Katherine Kroner  
Vice President, Advocacy and Patient Engagement
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Pulmonary Hypertension Association (PHA); signed by Katherine Kroner, Vice President, Advocacy and Patient Engagement
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group; Professional Association
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** PHA is described as the country's leading pulmonary hypertension organization, accrediting PH clinical programs, coordinating a national observational patient registry, providing continuing medical education, and serving patients, caregivers, and health care professionals.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

PHA supports CMS's effort to streamline electronic prior authorization for drugs, emphasizing that timely access to pulmonary hypertension therapies can be life-preserving. The comment urges CMS to impose rapid review timelines, transparent denial explanations, expert human review of AI denials, longer reauthorization periods, standardized forms, step therapy exceptions, recognition of prior payer determinations, and technology that reduces rather than compounds provider burden.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL/RFIs on step therapy and formulary access
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P. No CFR citations cited.
- **Standards referenced:** APIs, electronic medical records/electronic health records, artificial intelligence. No named FHIR IG, NCPDP, or HL7 standard is discussed.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic prior authorization for drug access**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** PH therapies are complex, time-sensitive, and often life-long. Electronic tracking and streamlining can improve patient access if EHRs can document PH-specific testing and workflows are clinically appropriate.
- **Specific request:** Ensure electronic PA systems handle complex testing such as echocardiograms and right heart catheterizations and support standardized, clinically relevant forms.

**Topic 2: Review timelines, appeals, and reauthorization**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Delays can worsen symptoms, extend hospital stays, cause mental distress, and in severe PH lead to irreversible decline or death.
- **Specific request:** Apply 48-hour standard and 24-hour expedited review recommendations, include urgent appeals and payer-provider interactions, require disease-expert appeals within no more than 72 hours, prohibit weekend information-request tactics, allow at least three to six months of continuity after plan changes, and extend stable-patient reauthorizations to every three to five years.

**Topic 3: Denial transparency and reviewer qualifications**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** Initial denials may lack clear reasons and appeal reviewers may lack PH expertise.
- **Specific request:** Require clear denial reasons, transparency about who conducts reviews, and automatic expert human review when AI issues an initial denial.

**Topic 4: Gold carding and reduced administrative burden**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Accredited PH centers frequently obtain eventual approval but spend substantial time overcoming administrative barriers.
- **Specific request:** Adopt gold carding for high-performing accredited centers, with eligibility based on eventual approval rather than first-submission approval.

**Topic 5: Step therapy exceptions and formulary access**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFIs
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy can force inappropriate treatment sequencing and delay needed therapy for a progressive, often fatal condition.
- **Specific request:** Require clear exceptions processes, 24-hour urgent and 72-hour normal responses, recognition of previous payer step therapy determinations, standardized exceptions processes, transparency of clinical reasoning, automatic expert human review of AI denials, and accessible real-time formulary information before plan selection.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** PHA identifies technical and clinical challenges for drug PA APIs, including EHR capability to document PH-specific testing and forms that request irrelevant data.
- **S15:** The comment describes PH therapies delivered by oral, inhaled, injected, and infusion routes, showing the complexity of benefit categorization, though it does not explicitly analyze medical versus pharmacy benefit boundaries.
- **S16/S17:** PHA asks for clear denial reasons, transparency about reviewers, and detailed appeal explanations.
- **S20/S43:** PHA supports 24-hour expedited and 48-hour standard review expectations, with urgent appeals and expert review completed promptly and within 72 hours where disease expertise is needed.
- **S21:** The comment supports electronic PA implementation but warns that systems must be clinically capable and integrated with EMR/EHR workflows.
- **S29/S35:** PHA supports electronic tracking of all prior authorizations and transparency, though it does not specify formal metric definitions.
- **S66-S82:** PHA responds to broader RFIs on step therapy, formulary information, technology, and AI review safeguards.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic prior authorization reforms in a way that improves timely PH drug access.
2. Require 48-hour standard review and 24-hour expedited review for urgent cases, including urgent appeals and payer-provider interactions.
3. Require disease-expert appeal review within no more than 72 hours when expert review is needed.
4. Prohibit payer tactics that request information when providers cannot reasonably respond and then use nonresponse to deny care.
5. Provide continuity for patients changing plans, ideally six months and at least three months before renewed authorization is required.
6. Extend stable-patient reauthorization intervals to three to five years for life-long PH therapies.
7. Ensure EHR and electronic PA systems can document PH-specific tests and support clinically relevant standardized forms.
8. Require clear denial reasons and transparency about reviewers for initial requests and appeals.
9. Require automatic expert human review of AI-generated denials.
10. Adopt gold carding for accredited centers based on eventual approval rates.
11. Provide real-time formulary information before plan selection.
12. Require standardized step therapy exception processes, recognition of prior payer determinations, and rapid exception timelines.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Treatment delays, irrelevant authorization requirements, unclear denials, insufficient reviewer expertise, frequent reauthorization, step therapy barriers, and AI denial safeguards.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Emergency room visits, functional decline, extended hospital stays, mental distress, irreversible disease progression, death, and higher long-term system costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Antiquated technology, poor EMR alignment, payer-by-payer form variation, outdated requirements, irrelevant test requests, appeal delays, scheduling barriers for peer-to-peer discussions, and inconsistent step therapy processes.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** 2023 PHA survey of 79 providers from 66 practices in 33 states; 72% saw 90% or more requests eventually approved; 48% of centers spent 20+ hours/week on PA and reauthorization; 12 centers spent 41-60 hours/week; 63% said PA often or always delayed care; reported impacts included extended hospital stays (80%), worsening symptoms from delayed or interrupted drugs (84%), and mental distress (91%).
- **Studies or research referenced:** PHA Accredited Care Centers survey; PHA registry and accreditation activities are described but not cited as a specific study.
- **Examples provided:** Around-the-clock infusion into the heart via pump, brand/generic sensitivity, renewals every six to twelve months disrupting stable therapy, weekend information requests, and step therapy repeat requirements after payer changes.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** PH patients, caregivers, PH specialists, accredited care centers, payers, reviewers, EHR vendors, and plans administering drug benefits.
- **Economic implications:** PHA argues delays increase long-term health system costs through hospital stays, emergency care, and more aggressive treatment needs; provider administrative time is substantial.
- **Technical feasibility:** Electronic PA is feasible and supported if systems can capture complex PH documentation, standardize clinically relevant forms, and integrate with provider workflows.
- **Patient care impact:** Very high; the comment repeatedly connects delayed access to worsening symptoms, irreversible decline, and possible death.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with significant modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, clinical, and urgent
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Delayed access to the most appropriate, highest impact treatment... can lead to loss of function" - Context: Explaining why PH prior authorization delays are dangerous.
2. "63% indicated that authorization requirements 'often' or 'always' delayed their patients' access to needed care." - Context: PHA survey evidence on care delays.
3. "PHA supports full transparency during the prior authorization process regarding who is conducting reviews... and clear reasons for any denials." - Context: Denial transparency recommendation.
4. "Technology should only be used to advance access to necessary medications for patients" - Context: Position on step therapy and technology.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - PHA requests 24-hour expedited, 48-hour standard, and 72-hour expert appeal timelines, plus longer reauthorization intervals.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment documents substantial staff time and argues delays increase long-term costs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - PHA emphasizes paperwork, varying requirements, irrelevant forms, and high weekly staff time.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment supports APIs and electronic tracking but stresses EHR capability and clinically fit forms.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Timely access to PH therapy is the central concern.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - PHA asks for clear denial reasons, reviewer transparency, formulary access, and appeal explanations.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment asks for EMR alignment, standardized forms, and efficient peer-to-peer and appeal processes.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Recommendations require coordination among CMS, payers, providers, expert reviewers, and technology vendors.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - PH therapies span oral, inhaled, injected, and infusion routes, creating benefit-design complexity.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Not framed as equity in detail, but improved access and plan-selection formulary transparency may reduce unequal access.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Not addressed directly.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed directly.
